newsitem.title: USA: "Witch" is potential juror in Oklahoma bomb case.
newsitem.headline: "Witch" is potential juror in Oklahoma bomb case.

text.p: A potential juror in the Oklahoma City bombing trial on Thursday surprised the courtroom when she described herself as a witch who believes in paganism.

The young mother, whose husband committed suicide in 1993, said she could set aside her reservations about the death penalty and would consider it as a possible punishment for accused bomber Timothy McVeigh if he were convicted.
McVeigh, who is accused of bombing the Alfred P. Murrah federal building on April 19, 1995, killing 168 people, faces death if found guilty. He has pleaded innocent to the bombing.
The woman, who has studied graphic art, said she attended "circles" where people burned incense, danced and sang.
The soft-spoken woman, who paused several times before answering questions, said she first learned about being a witch when she was 12 years old.
"I began to get interested in ghosts and spirits and started reading about paganism," she said, adding that she decided to become a witch after graduating from high school.

The woman said she was raised a Christian and described the Wicca "religion" as a peaceful one whose adherents worshipped gods and goddesses. A Wiccan is a member of a group that practices witchcraft.

"Love for others, understanding before judgment, peace with the earth, joy and happiness with yourself, more spiritual views than material (ones)," was the list she gave when asked to describe the beliefs of her group.
Initially, she said the death penalty was never justified but when pressed by prosecutor Larry Mackey the woman said she could set aside her views and vote for the death penalty.
About 55 people have been questioned by the judge, prosecutors and defence attorneys as they try to select a jury of 12 plus six alternates.

The judge has indicated on several occasions he is ready to accommodate potential jurors. On Thursday, he told a divorced mother he would be prepared to recess court to allow her to attend her son's graduation ceremony on May 20.
"There can be situations where we can recess to accommodate a particular juror's event, like that. It's not impossible," Matsch told her.
